terrain.difficultyNotes: Pico publishes a three-tier split as trail counts - 10 easier, 26 more difficult, 21 most difficult out of 58 - so percentExpert is null and the 36% top tier sits in percentAdvanced. Note the base elevation: at 2,000 feet Pico starts higher than most Vermont resorts, which is why it holds snow better than its size suggests. The 468-acre figure is the same one Killington’s combined stats page attributes to Pico.

Note the asymmetry regulars all know: most passes bought for Killington are valid at Pico, but a Pico pass is not valid at Killington.

editorial.overview: Pico is what Killington would be if it had never become The Beast, and it sits three miles down the road as a permanent reminder. Nearly 2,000 feet of vertical - within a hundred feet of Killington’s lift-served drop on the trails that matter - 58 trails, six lifts, and a base lodge you can park next to. It is owned and operated by Killington, sold on the same Ikon allocation, and almost entirely ignored by the people who fill Killington’s gondola queue every Saturday. The skiing is genuinely good. The 49er is a long summit blue steeper than anything on Killington’s lower mountain, Giant Killer is a legitimately fearsome double black that is perennially icy and technical, and the Summit Glades are all-natural, ungroomed, and hold some of the biggest bumps in central Vermont. Pico’s weakness is operational rather than geographic: it does not open every day of the week in early and late season, it has no village and limited food, and the Summit Express does not always run when the lower mountain does. Treat it as a mountain to check the operating schedule for rather than turn up at, and it repays the effort with the shortest lift lines you will find on 2,000 vertical feet anywhere in Vermont.
editorial.snowQuality: Pico’s claimed 250 inches of natural snow matches Killington’s, which makes sense - they are the same massif - but Pico starts at 2,000 feet, the highest base elevation of any resort in this guide. That matters more than the snowfall number: storms that fall as rain at Killington’s 1,165-foot Skyeship base fall as snow at Pico’s base lodge, and the bottom of the mountain stays skiable through marginal weather that turns Killington’s runouts to slush. Snowmaking covers 75%, enough to keep the main trails reliable. The Summit Glades are natural only and need real cover, which combined with the intermittent Summit Express operation means the best terrain here is the least dependable.
editorial.crowds: The emptiest 2,000-foot mountain in Vermont, and it is not close. Everyone who might otherwise ski Pico is three miles away at Killington, so the Golden Express and Summit Express run with empty chairs on days when Killington’s K-1 gondola has a twenty-five minute queue. The catch is that Pico is not always open - it has run limited midweek operations in some seasons, and the Summit Express is the first thing to stop spinning - so the absence of crowds is partly the absence of an operating mountain. When it is fully open on a weekend it is the best-value lift-served skiing in central Vermont. Check the schedule before driving.
editorial.difficulty: Pico rates honestly and skis harder than its trail count implies. Thirty-six percent of the trails are in the top tier, and Giant Killer earns its name - the steepest trail on the mountain, perennially icy, with rocks and technical features that make it a genuine test rather than a steep groomer. Sunset 71 is a real black off the summit and the 49er is a blue that would be a black at Okemo. The Summit Glades are the standout: all natural, all ungroomed, with tree islands and the biggest bumps here. What Pico lacks is volume - the hard terrain is a handful of trails rather than a network - and a nervous intermediate should be careful about the summit, because the ways down from the top are not gentle.

keyTrails.name: Giant Killer
keyTrails.note: The steepest trail on the mountain and perennially icy, with rocks and technical features. A genuine double black that catches people out who came expecting a quiet little hill.

keyTrails.name: Summit Glades
keyTrails.note: All natural, all ungroomed, with islands of trees and the biggest bumps at Pico. The reason strong skiers make the trip.

keyTrails.name: 49er
keyTrails.note: An expansive summit blue that is steeper than anything on the lower mountain, and the trail that shows Pico is a real mountain rather than an annex.

keyTrails.name: Sunset 71
keyTrails.note: A winding black off the summit with a proper fall line and, usually, nobody on it.

keyTrails.name: Pike
keyTrails.note: Pico’s longest trail, running more than a mile from the summit to the base lodge. The civilised way down.

tidbits: Pico’s 1,967-foot vertical drop is within a hundred feet of Killington’s, on a mountain with a fraction of the traffic.
At 2,000 feet, Pico has the highest base elevation of any resort in this guide.
Pico is owned and operated by Killington and shares its Ikon Pass allocation - a day at both counts as one day.
Most passes bought for Killington are valid at Pico, but a Pico pass is not valid at Killington.
The resort’s terrain parks are Prospector and Panhandler, off the Golden Express.
bestFor: High base elevation in a thaw
watchOutFor: Summit Express does not always run

reviews.gist: Lifts and facilities both 8/10, with well-groomed cruisers across the mountain and the crowd relief that comes from sitting next to Killington. The operational catch is the one that matters: closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays outside holiday weeks, secondary lifts run inconsistently, and Forty Niner still gets congested despite the low visitation.

Twelfth in the East, above Okemo, Stratton and Mount Snow — all three of them larger operations with more lifts. On a snow-weighted system Pico’s elevation is what carries it, and it is the highest base elevation in this guide.

moguls.policy: The Summit Glades are all natural and never groomed, which is where Pico’s bumps live. The marked trails off the Golden Express are groomed conventionally, so the mountain has a clear split between a groomed lower half and an ungroomed summit.

namedRuns.name: Summit Glades
namedRuns.note: All natural, all ungroomed, with islands of trees. Skier consensus is that these hold the best and biggest bumps on the mountain by a wide margin.

namedRuns.name: Giant Killer
namedRuns.note: The steepest trail at Pico. Bumps form on it, but it is perennially icy and the troughs glaze hard - this is a bump run for people who like a fight.

namedRuns.name: Sunset 71
namedRuns.note: A winding summit black that bumps up between grooming passes, and is quiet enough that what forms survives.

moguls.quality: Better than a mountain this obscure has any right to have. The Summit Glades combine natural snow, no grooming and almost no traffic, which is the recipe for well-formed bumps that last, and the tree islands break the pitch up so the lines have variety rather than being one long trough. The catch is access: the Summit Express does not run every day Pico is open, and when it is down the glade bumps are unreachable. Giant Killer is the other bump option and is a much less pleasant one - skier consensus is consistent that it is icy more often than not.
moguls.bestTiming: A few days after a storm when the Summit Express is running and the natural cover is deep. Spring, when the ice on Giant Killer finally softens, is the other window.
moguls.bumpCulture: None. Pico has no competitions and no organised scene - the mountain barely markets itself at all, which is part of its appeal.

parks.name: Prospector
parks.note: One of the two parks off the Golden Express, with a mix of jumps, rails and boxes maintained for a range of abilities.

parks.name: Panhandler
parks.note: The smaller of Pico’s two parks and the natural starting point, alongside Prospector on the same side of the mountain.

parks.progression: Two parks side by side off the Golden Express, Panhandler feeding Prospector. No airbag, no coaching programme, no branded facility.
parks.overview: A modest two-park setup on a mountain that is not trying to be a park destination. Adequate for a local rider working on basics, and pleasantly empty.
parks.reputation: Not a park mountain and does not claim to be. Anyone in central Vermont who rides park seriously drives the three miles to Killington, which runs eight parks and a Burton tree park; Pico’s two exist to serve its own visitors rather than to compete.
